(p-691) Surah "Al-Masad" (The Palm Fiber)

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he.﴾ "Al-tabab" means destruction (halak), and from it comes their saying: "Is she a young woman (ashabbah) or a woman past childbearing (tabbah)?", meaning: destroyed by old age. The meaning is: his hands perished, because—as is narrated—he took a stone to throw at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

﴿And he perished﴾: his whole self perished, or his hands were made to be perishing, and what is meant is the destruction of his entire being, as in His saying: ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [al-Hajj: 10]. The meaning of "and he perished" is: that occurred and took place, as in the verse of the poet:

"May Allah repay him with the worst of his recompense... the recompense of the snarling dogs, and he has done it."

The reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, "and he has indeed perished" (qad tabba), also indicates this. It is narrated that when ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214] was revealed, he (ﷺ) ascended al-Safa and called out: "Yā ṣabāḥāh!" (Alas, morning!), so the people gathered to him from every direction. He ﷺ said: "O sons of Abd al-Muttalib, O sons of Fihr, if I informed you that there are horsemen at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a terrible punishment." Abu Lahab said: "Destruction to you! Is it for this that you summoned us?!" So this surah was revealed. He was given the kunya (teknonym) rather than his name, and honouring by kunya is a mark of respect, because he was known by it rather than by his name; or because his name was disliked, for his name was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā; or because his end would be a fire of flame, so his condition matched his kunya, "Abu Lahab."

Makkī.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 111, verse 2:

﴿His wealth did not avail him, nor what he earned.﴾ "Ma" (what) here is for negation.

﴿And what he earned﴾: it is in the nominative case (marfu'), and "ma" is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). The meaning is "and what was earned by him" or "and his earning," i.e., his wealth did not benefit him, whether the wealth he inherited from his father or the wealth he earned by himself, or his inherited wealth (al-talid) and his newly acquired wealth (al-tarif).

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "What he earned: his child." It is narrated that he (Abu Lahab) used to say: "If what my nephew says is true, then I will ransom myself from it with my wealth and my children."

﴿سَيَصْلى نارًا﴾: "He will burn in a Fire." (Sa-yasla), he will enter (sa-yadkhulu). "Sa-yuṣlā" (read with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ*), transmitted by al-Burjumī from Abū Bakr (a *qirāʾah*, variant recitation). The *sīn* indicates a threat (*waʿīd*), meaning: it is certain to happen, though its time may be delayed.

﴿ذاتَ لَهَبٍ﴾: "of blazing flame," blazing (tawaqqadu).

**Verse 4:** ﴿And his wife﴾ is Umm Jamil bint Harb, the sister of Abu Sufyan,

﴿the carrier of firewood﴾. She used to carry a bundle of thorns and thistle-spines and scatter them at night on the path of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: she used to walk about carrying tale-bearing (namimah), kindling the fire of enmity among people. ʿĀṣim read "ḥammālata al-ḥaṭab" in the accusative, as a form of vituperation (shatm). I myself love this reading, and it was by the beauty of [this reading] that one may draw near to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by reviling Umm Jamil. On this reading, it is permissible to pause at "wa-imra'atuhu," because it is conjoined to the pronoun in "sayaṣlā" (i.e., "he and his wife will enter [the Fire]"). The implied construction is: "I mean, the carrier of firewood." Others read it in the nominative, "ḥammālatu al-ḥaṭab," as the predicate of "wa-imra'atuhu," or [as in the sense of] "she is a carrier."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 111, verse 5:

﴿فِي جِيدِها حَبْلٌ مِن مَسَدٍ﴾ ("Around her neck is a rope of twisted fiber"): this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or another predicate (khabar). "Al-masad" (al-masad, the twisted rope) is that which is tightly twisted from ropes, whether of palm fiber, hide, or other materials. The meaning is: "Around her neck is a rope made of what has been twisted from ropes," and that she carries that bundle of thorns and ties it around her neck, as woodcutters do, to belittle her and to depict her in the image of some wood-gathering women, so that she will be distressed by this, and her husband will be distressed too, though they are in a house of honor and nobility, and in a station of wealth and prosperity.
